I think healthy skepticism is a good thing, especially when it comes to news. If not for ethical reasons then to avoid surrounding ourselves with sources that only feed our existing opinions. News can be neutral, of course, and I think a neutral statement of the facts should be valued in reporting.

To more directly answer your question of reviews, there are some sites I'll seek reviews on more than others - Co-optimus is one just because they analyze games with co-op in mind, which is often what I'm most interested in. But I think it's also worth remembering that reviewers might not always have the same considerations for a game that you do, so having specific questions in mind can be helpful when you're researching a game. Do you have bandwidth concerns, how important is a bug-free experience, and is a rich story a priority?

All in all I think yours is a good question to be asking because by critically evaluating the way we get news, we can do a better job of identifying what it is we value in a game and which games match those values. Good post!

There are ways to identify dishonest reviews. It's fortunate for readers that most of the reviewers who would falsify sentiments about a game are also not particularly talented writers. They'll tend to contradict themselves, which is a sure sign their review is questionable whether they're being intentionally misleading or not. I regularly point out poorly written articles that get posted here. It's not worth getting worked up over whether they're being honest or not. I can't trust someone's ability to interpret and quantify anything about a game if they had 12+ years of formal education and still haven't learned the language they speak every day.

There's no such thing as a site where you can trust the articles 100% of the time. We have to learn to put 2 and 2 together for ourselves. For example, I find it a lot easier to trust reviews that mention things that worked and things that didn't work, with a focus on things that matter. People who are exclusively positive or negative about a game aren't being objective, and objectivity is the main thing a review needs to have.

Reviewing games is not easy. Some people aren't cut out for it, but most people can learn to do it if they're willing to learn. It's the ones who aren't seeing success and are getting desperate that are the most likely to let their reviews be influenced by outside sources. If you can spot the reviewers who don't really know what they're doing, you already know who to avoid whether they're dishonest or not.

The article linked is merely a hit piece on social security, and while it never clearly crosses the factual line, treads too close to it to be credible.

A key to this is understanding the sentence "Social Security has long been sold to the public on the notion that what a worker will receive back is what he or she pays into the system." This is not in fact how "Social Security" works -- the writers know that -- but they are choosing not to dispel this notion but rather repeat the falsehood and hammer on fears of insolvency and cherry-picked facts meant to stir the indignation of tax-haters.

To state what the writer should have: "Social Security" is not a pension fund into which you put your money when you are young and withdraw it when you are old. To the contrary, it is an INSTANT transfer from workers to retirees. That's why the first-ever participants mentioned in the article (Ida May Fuller, for example) were able to receive benefits but had never "paid into the system." Nobody "pays into the system" and never has.

It can also never go "bankrupt" -- the "Social Security Trust Fund" that everyone talks about running out (in 2035, or whenever) is NOT part of the transfer payments. It is EXCESS RESERVES that resulted from over-taxation in the past. Naturally people worry about it being depleted, because "running out of money" is something people understand -- but this fear is misplaced.

I am not at all worried about Social Security funding. Can you imagine the political lightning rod that Social Security will be in 2030? By that time 25% of the US population will be over 65. If there's a truth about politics, it's that old people vote, and old people want their SS benefits.
